newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Court rejects opposition victory in Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Court rejects opposition victory in Belgrade.

text.p: A Belgrade municipal court has upheld a previous decision rejecting an election victory by Serbia's opposition in the capital, an electoral commission official said on Monday.
The First District Court dismissed appeals from the city's electoral commission demanding the recognition of the opposition victory, commission chief Radomir Lazarevic said.

Court annulments of opposition victories in municipal elections have prompted more than two months of street protests in Serbia that have grown into demands for an end to President Slobodan Milosevic's authoritarian rule.

The city electoral commission had confirmed the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition won a majority in the Belgrade municipal assembly but the courts, under the control of ruling Socialists, overturned the commission's decision.
A clearly angry Lazarevic informed a student delegation of the decision in a meeting witnessed by reporters.
"The decision is completely against the law," Lazarevic said.
The electoral commission may have exhausted all legal avenues and will meet on Tuesday to discuss its next move, he said.
"I don't have another country to live in. This is my only country and I wish that all of this is solved as soon as possible and according to the law."
He said the authorities had given Serbian people good cause for their daily protests.
"Truth and justice are endangered. There is a legal right of the people to start a rebellion," he said.
Belgrade analysts said the court decision may set the stage for a political confrontation in which the opposition and the ruling Socialists would attempt to form rival city governments.
With its legal options spent, the city commission may choose to formally confirm the opposition's mandate, allowing it to constitute a new municipal government despite the court rulings.
The ruling Socialists may also decide to form their own version of the municipal assembly.
After previous appeals were rejected by the courts, the electoral commission's latest appeal had demanded that the Supreme Court review the entire matter.
The commission had alleged that municipal court judges, First District Court judges and the acting president of the Supreme Court had issued rulings without legal foundation.
Instead, the First District court dismissed the commission's appeals, aggravating political deadlock between the Zajedno coalition and Milosevic's Socialists.
Opposition leaders have accused Milosevic of using the courts to sow confusion and delay any clear resolution of the crisis.
Lazarevic promised the student delegation, led by Cedomir Jovanovic, to deliver records of all objections submitted by all parties since the run-off polls were held on November 17.
An expert commission sent by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe had also agreed with the commission's conclusions on ballot results in Belgrade, Lazarevic said.

When one of the university students asked what student protesters could do to help with the commission's work, Lazarevic replied: "Thank you very much but the only person who can help us is God himself."
